title: The demand for factors of production

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Explain what the demand for a factor of production is, where it comes from, and what makes it rise or fall.

blocks.heading: What firms ask for when they hire
blocks.text: The demand for a factor of production is the quantity of a factor - land, labour, capital or enterprise, the four factors introduced in topic 1.2 - that firms are willing and able to employ at a given cost over a period of time. Otjiwa Dairy near Gobabis demands milkers, drivers and refrigeration tanks because it expects to sell dairy products; a cheese maker in the Netherlands demands cheesemakers and ageing cellars for the same reason.

blocks.heading: Derived demand: where it comes from
blocks.text: Factor demand is a derived demand: firms want workers and machines for the sake of the goods those inputs produce, not for the inputs themselves. When Kaoko Juice of Oshakati wins a contract to supply schools, its need for fruit-handlers and bottling staff rises with it; when a lodge near Etosha loses visitors, it takes on fewer guides. The chain runs: consumers demand more juice -> the firm needs more inputs to fill the orders -> its demand for labour rises.

blocks.heading: What shifts it
blocks.text: Four influences move a firm's factor demand. Demand for the product: a stronger market for the good tends to raise the firm's demand for the factors that make it. The price of the factor: a higher wage tends to make a firm cautious about hiring, and where equipment can do the work at lower cost per unit, the firm may employ fewer workers and more capital. Availability: where a factor is scarce in an area - bricklayers in a remote town, flat land near a port, or machines that must be imported and wait months for spare parts - the firm may be unable to employ as much as it wants and may turn to factors that are easier to obtain. A building firm in a town where few skilled bricklayers live may use precast concrete panels that need fewer of them. A factor in plentiful supply tends to be cheaper and quicker to employ. Productivity: a more productive factor produces more for each N$ spent on it, so firms tend to prefer it to less productive alternatives - a trained machinist over an untrained one at a similar wage, a fast machine over a slow one. Yet where each worker produces more, fewer workers may cover the same orders, though a busy firm with growing sales may still take people on.

blocks.heading: Two different demands
blocks.text: Learners often treat the demand for factors as if it behaved like the demand for goods. The boundary: consumers demand goods for the satisfaction they give; firms demand factors to produce output that others buy. The test is to ask who is buying and for what - a household buying juice is demanding a good, whereas the juice firm hiring fruit-handlers is demanding a factor. The driver differs too: a consumer's demand moves with tastes, incomes and price, while a firm's factor demand moves with the demand for its product.
